verses.2: Keep vigil through most of the night.
verses.3: Half the night, or a little less.
verses.4: Or a little more; recite the Qur’an in measure.
verses.5: Soon, a weighty word will be cast upon you.
verses.6: Al-Mizan says night is steadier and speech sounder, whereas daytime is a long immersion.
verses.7: Al-Mizan says night is steadier and speech sounder, whereas daytime is a long immersion.
verses.8: Remember your Lord and devote yourself wholly to Him.
verses.9: The east-and-west Lord alone is God; take Him as trustee.
verses.10: Be patient with what they say and withdraw gracefully.
verses.11: Leave the prosperous deniers to Me briefly.
verses.12: Al-Mizan warns of heavy fetters, fierce fire, choking food, and painful punishment.
verses.13: Al-Mizan warns of heavy fetters, fierce fire, choking food, and painful punishment.
verses.14: Al-Mizan foretells earth and mountains quaking, with mountains becoming running dunes of sand.
verses.15: Al-Mizan says a messenger was sent as witness, as one was sent to Pharaoh.
verses.16: Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger and was terribly seized.
verses.17: How will disbelievers escape the day that whitens children’s hair?
verses.18: The heaven will split thereby; God’s promise is certain.
verses.19: Al-Mizan introduces this as an early Meccan sūrah—possibly the second or third revealed, among the al-ʿatāʾiq—which prepares the Prophet for the Qur’an’s weight through night prayer, commands patience under accusations of poetry, soothsaying, and madness, and warns the disbelievers; the opening directives are later extended to believers and reduced in the final verse. “O you wrapped up” simply addresses the Prophet wrapped in a garment to sleep after the derision and sorrow confronting his call; it neither praises nor reproaches him. The ensuing command directs him to prayer and patience rather than retreating into sleep, and the claim that he is wrapped in the raiment of prophethood lacks textual evidence. “Stand” means establish the night prayer, with half the night, a little less, or a little more as genuine alternatives. A reading that treats these measures as the exception has the same result, while a reading allowing exceptions for illness or sleep is sound but less immediate. Tartīl means clear, successive articulation of the Qur’an’s letters; it is a parallel command, apparently for recitation in ritual prayer, though some make it independent recitation. The “weighty word” is the Glorious Qur’an. It is weighty in its divine meanings, which require a soul purified and detached from all but God, and in realizing its teachings and bearing the mission of pure monotheism; its effect on the Prophet is reflected in numerous reports of buraḥāʾ al-waḥy, the intensity of revelation. It is also weighty because it makes the Prophet and his ummah endure propagation, opposition, and obedience according to each person’s capacity. The Qur’an’s own descriptions as clarification of all things (16:89), able to humble a mountain (59:21), and supreme in power (13:31) support this reading. Other descriptions—solid speech, weight in the Resurrection balance, hardship for deniers, or enduring permanence—may be sound, but are less apparent. Night vigil prepares the Prophet for proximity, presence, and such revelation; (73:19) and (76:29), together with (17:79), identify it as a way to the Lord. Al-Mizan understands nāshiʾat al-layl as the night itself, or possibly prayer at night: freedom from daytime occupations steadies the person and makes speech more accurate, or heart and tongue more harmonious under the alternative wiṭʾan reading. Sabḥ by day is total immersion in life’s demands. It finds this contextual explanation superior to the claims that daytime merely supplies sleep and affairs or makes up missed night worship. Remembering the Lord’s name continues the night-prayer command, chiefly verbal dhikr accompanied by the heart, and tabattul is complete detachment for God; reports from the Ahl al-Bayt take it as raising the hands and humbly entreating. A generalized command to verbal remembrance is possible, but a general command to inner remembrance is not; yet Al-Mizan rejects the premise that unceasing remembrance is impossible, arguing that God never truly leaves anyone and that the angels’ unwearied glorification ((41:38); (21:20)) is not unique to them. “Your Lord” turns from the majestic first person to a reminder of creaturely servitude, and tabtīlan can express the force of tabattul or preserve the verses’ rhyme. God’s lordship over east and west encompasses the universe and grounds His sole ulūhiyyah: since He alone directs all affairs, He alone is worshipped. Taking Him as wakīl means, outwardly, using the means He provides without treating any as independent causes and leaving results to Him, and, legislatively, subordinating one’s choice to His rulings; these two aspects respectively ground the following endurance of abuse and the preceding commands. Patience and graceful withdrawal require good manners, sincere invitation, and no retaliation, not an abrogation by jihad. God’s command to leave Him with the wealthy deniers threatens their ungratefulness for His gifts: their worldly respite is short before reckoning and torment. It is general, not an evident allusion to Badr; the shift to “Me” intensifies the threat, and “Us” in the next verse signals majesty. The fetters, fierce fire, choking food, and painful punishment are the hereafter’s replacement for their worldly enjoyment. The quaking earth and mountains turned into running dunes identify the time of this punishment. The audience is then directly warned through Pharaoh: just as Moses was sent to Pharaoh, Muḥammad is sent as witness to his people’s actions in this world and the next. Pharaoh’s terrible seizure followed disobedience to a messenger as God’s messenger, not to an ordinary man; his power, army, kingdom, and authority could not defend him. The day that makes children white-headed evokes the punishment’s severity, not its duration, and the heaven’s splitting may occur in or because of that terrible day; God’s promise is fixed. Finally, tadhkirah is the preceding warning and admonition, and taking a way to the Lord means correct belief and practical obedience. Al-Mizan also judges that “this” can point specifically to the opening night-prayer command, thereby extending it from the Prophet to whoever wills; its repetition after mention of night prayer in (76:29) makes that prayer a distinctive path to God.
verses.20: Al-Mizan reads (73:20) as reducing the night-vigil burden imposed at the sūrah’s opening and extended to believers in (73:19): the instruction to recite as much of the Qur’an as is feasible does not make a third, half, or nearly two-thirds of the night forbidden. Although reports date the verse in Mecca eight months, one year, or ten years after the rest of the sūrah, it considers the verse apparently Medinan. Its specified zakāt is the religious due legislated after the migration, not an unproved Meccan obligation later quantified or an obligation mentioned before its legislation; its reference to jihad likewise does not suit the Meccan circumstances. Addressing God as “your Lord” conveys mercy and grace, while His knowing that the Prophet stands vigil expresses gratitude, as (76:22) does. Adnā means slightly less than two-thirds, and “or” distributes the different measures over different nights. The group “with you” shares īmān with the Prophet, and min is partitive: some believers, not a merely descriptive “group,” kept the vigil with him. Allah’s measuring night and day explains His knowledge of every measure; taqdīr belongs to His creative act. Iḥṣāʾ is full grasping and measuring, whether of that measurement or of the prescribed vigil itself, which most believers cannot reliably span as night lengths change and waking for a precise portion is difficult. God’s tawbah is His prior merciful turning toward servants: it enables their repentance and obedience and may reduce obligations; after their repentance, His further tawbah remits sins (9:118). The fāʾ connecting this knowledge to feasible recitation therefore lowers the requirement for the community as a whole, though some, including the Prophet, can bear the longer periods; it does not cancel the original command for those able and willing to undertake it. The opening command is apparently obligatory for the Prophet and supererogatory for other believers. Al-Mizan notes but declines lengthy treatment of disputes over whether the vigil is prayer or independent recitation, who is bound by it, and whether it was abrogated or merely reduced. A translator’s note qualifies the author’s narrow uṣūl definition of naskh: in the Qur’anic sense, this very change may be abrogation, meaning a provisional rule’s practical requirements cease without the revealed verse becoming useless; (2:106) and (16:101) show that sharīʿah injunctions and early Muslim practice are not immutable. Illness, travel for trade, and fighting in God’s way give further reasons for relief. The repetition of feasible recitation confirms that vigil is to match one’s time and circumstances; “of it” refers to the Qur’an. Prayer and zakāt remain obligatory—five daily prayers if the verse is Medinan, or the prescribed prayer then current if Meccan—while lending God a good loan is financial charity beyond zakāt. Thus easing the vigil does not relax other duties, as the comparison with (58:13) shows. “Good” covers every obligatory and supererogatory act of obedience sent ahead for one’s eternal life. Huwa may emphatically repeat the preceding pronoun or introduce the predicate, but either way such deeds are preserved with God and found better and greater in reward than what one did or renounced. Seeking forgiveness is promised by the Ever-Forgiving, Ever-Merciful and plausibly includes every act of obedience, since obedience is a means to forgiveness and may itself be called istighfār.
